deep.reconstruction:
The page has no derivation, formula or computation. It is an experimental or observational sheet in physiological optics. What is on it:

(a) A long ruled pencil line along the right side, with cross-marks at both ends, captioned 'Höhe des Auges über der Ebene des Papiers' ('height of the eye above the plane of the paper'). The segment is a length scale: it records the distance h at which the eye was held perpendicularly above the sheet.

(b) A small circle near the centre of the sheet. It is either a fixation point or an archival or paper mark; I cannot tell which.

(c) Two irregular closed pencil outlines, one above and one below the centre. The caption runs along the long edge, so the sheet was meant to be turned 90°. Turned that way, the two outlines lie left and right of the central point at roughly equal distances.

My interpretation (not stated on the page): this is a map of the two blind spots (Mariotte spots), one per eye. The procedure would be to hold the eye at height h above the central fixation point and trace on the paper the boundary where a moving pencil tip vanishes.

Rough measurements from the image (mine, approximate):
- Scale segment: about 1475 px.
- Distance from the central point to each outline's centre: about 475–490 px.
- Angular eccentricity: arctan(480/1475) ≈ 18°.
- Outline extent: about 280–320 px. Allowing for oblique projection (a factor of about cos²θ), this is about 10° of visual angle.

The eccentricity is close to the standard blind-spot position of about 15° temporal. The outlines are irregular and roughly oval, as blind-spot maps usually are. This supports the reading, though the outlines are somewhat larger than typical textbook values (about 5.5° × 7.5°).

The page offers nothing further to restate mathematically.
errors: The blind-spot reading is an inference: the eccentricity of about 18° fits, but the outlines are larger than the usual angular size of the optic disc. The sheet could instead be a different perceptual or perspective experiment, e.g. apparent shapes seen from a fixed eye point.

results.what: Plotting the outlines of a region on paper as seen from an eye at a recorded height above the sheet; plausibly mapping the blind spots of the two eyes around a fixation point
results.usually_credited_to: Mariotte (discovery, 1660s); systematic mapping in 19th-century physiological optics (e.g. Helmholtz, Handbuch der physiologischen Optik, 1856–67; Listing, Volkmann)
